title: Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril | George Monbiot
desc: If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poor  However grim the trajectory might seem, I’ve always believed that sense will ultimately prevail. As the great perils of dismantling the living world become increasingly obvious, even the most rapacious exploiters must come round. Nobody wants to live on a dead planet, do they?There are – or were – signs that this wasn’t just wishful thinking. Since 2015, mostly thanks to China, the area of the planet being reforested has increased, while thanks in large part to Brazil, the global rate of forest destruction has declined. The area of the Brazilian Amazon forest cleared each year is one-sixth of what it was when records began in 1988. In the past four years, as a result of Brazilian government policy, the deforestation rate has fallen by 71%. desc: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/NintendoBringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video gameWhen the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I was frankly delighted. My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto.Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. title: Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad taste

Broad and crass as it often is – in fact always is – this Ali G sequel is sometimes funny: the athletic vigour of our hero’s pranking and punking is like the umpteenth Jackass film at which you might find yourself laughing, and Baron Cohen blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed.Unlike the first film, Ali G in Da House from 2002, this is not a full written-through narrative. It is basically another live-ammo series of hoaxes with some spectacular bad taste perpetrated upon the deserving and less deserving; it satirises the shamelessness of anti-woke free speech martyrs, punching up and down with grossout cringe, and the targets include some big names who shouldn’t be revealed here. There are two other subordinate characters: Erran Morad, a sinister Mossad/IDF officer turned US security consultant (who appeared in Baron Cohen’s Who Is America? TV series), and a new figure: Dr Nira Cain-N’Degrocello, a grotesquely supercilious white liberal who is the self-appointed scourge of cultural appropriation. The dupes are built into a big silly climax fabricated with body doubles and (presumably) covert reshooting. Continue reading...

title: Proms, parties and gender politics: amazing photos from American dancefloors – and what they tell us about a changing nation
desc:
From George Balanchine to the Rockettes, the US magazine regularly ran lavish photo spreads dedicated to dance, with the myriad ways people moved their bodies holding up a mirror to the shifting timesLife magazine launched in 1936. Its aim: to show the US the world, in pictures. At a time when television was still an experimental medium, a golden age of photojournalism brought the outside world into people’s homes. Life ran weekly until 1972, spanning a transformative time in US culture. Photographers were dispatched across the globe, covering wars, political manoeuvres, social trends, hemlines and Hollywood. And in December 1936, the magazine dedicated its cover feature to dance, with dancers from the new School of American Ballet gracing the front page. As such a vividly visual medium, dance would become a regular feature in Life’s pages across the years.
 
 
 When I was asked to write the text for a new book featuring a collection of dance-themed images from the Life archive, it was a kid-in-a-candy-shop situation. For a dance fan there were some absolute gems to be found: the great George Balanchine crafting his ballet The Seven Deadly Sins – and cooking dinner in his Manhattan apartment; Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev taking New York in a piece headlined The Hottest Little Team in Show Biz; or an ageing Agnes de Mille going full-throttle in rehearsal.But the archive told a much bigger story than that. It was fascinating to see the reflection of society through the way people danced: in ballrooms, nightclubs, proms and parties. In the array of social dancers: from the waltz and tango to the lindy hop, mambo, twist and the frug, themes of the 20th century play out. You can see a story of growing individualism in the shift from structured couple dancing to going freeform on the dancefloor – gender politics, too, as it was out with “May I have this dance?” and in with the democracy of the disco. Life columnist Albert Goldman asked: “Has there ever been a decade for dance like the 60s?” as he wrote of a power shift from the stage to the dancefloor, from the professional performer to the “inventive amateur”. There’s the birth of the teenager, too, bringing an explosion of pop culture and spreading dance trends on TV shows such as American Bandstand. Continue reading...

title: ‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the Sun
desc: The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?In the wings of the London film festival, a group of young influencers are discussing their personal highlights. Klara and the Sun, says one, and her colleagues agree. It’s not just that the film is still so fresh in their memory, or that they have gathered today to meet its creators and stars. Klara is funny and moving; it’s their festival favourite so far. I relay this exchange to Taika Waititi, the film’s director, who is sipping bottled water in a room down the hall. His gaze widens. He almost chokes. “Thank God!” he exclaims with just a bit too much heat.Everybody has a perfect film, just as everybody has a perfect friend, and they vary because everybody is different. In the film, sick 14-year-old Josie loves her discontinued robot doll Klara, whereas most kids her age opt for brighter, shinier models. And the young influencers love Klara and the Sun – Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel – while most older critics vehemently, violently disagree. All of which shows that there’s no accounting for taste, that people are confounding, and that our hearts and our brains are not always in sync. That keeps life interesting. It’s partly what the film is about. “The emotions that we give very simple labels to are really complex,” says Ishiguro, who is seated alongside the director. “The thing we call love, for example, is incredibly noisy and multifaceted. title: Shovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom
desc: (tak:til)The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its presentThose thus far unaware of Shovel Dance Collective’s bracing approach to folk should probably note that their third album is not much interested in breaking newcomers in gently. Everything in Readiness kicks off with a three-song suite that lasts more than 10 minutes and takes you, via a series of dramatic sonic jump-cuts, from a grinding one-note drone to a reel that seems to split the difference between trad folk fiddle-playing and the punishing squall of the Velvet Underground’s Black Angel’s Death Song. It then leaps to Tally Ho! Hark Away!, which sets a hunting song first collected in the late 1940s over a blast of what might best be described as ecstatic noise. It’s genuinely hard to work out what instruments are involved in the clattering arrhythmic chaos behind the vocal – there’s definitely a heavily distorted guitar in the mix – but the effect is weirdly euphoric rather than claustrophobic: a kind of purgative release after the mounting weirdness of the preceding reel.If you’re looking for evidence that the nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to folk music, then there it is. The glib shorthand is that they’re doing for traditional English music what Lankum have done for its Irish equivalent – joining the dots with the kind of out-there experimentation that fills the pages of the Wire magazine – although it should be pointed out they sound almost nothing like Lankum. Anyone who already has an interest in leftfield explorations of British musical history might suggest their chaotic collage approach feels more akin to the fascinating collections of field recordings, folk song and avant garde composition released by Todmorden-based label Folklore Tapes. The music on Everything in Readiness careens unpredictably from gentle lo-fi recordings caked in distortion and tape hiss to the tumultuous, surging racket they serve up on their version of the traditional coalminer’s song Jowl, Jowl and Listen; from singing unaccompanied by anything but the sound of birdsong to the disquieting ambient shimmer of Who Killed Cock Robin? A Summoning (Kind Morning in our Fists), which sounds like it was recorded in a vast, echoing crypt. Continue reading...

title: Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra / Wigglesworth review – phrasing with hospital corners
desc: Lighthouse, PooleBSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burn On paper, it was a curious programme: Tippett’s Concerto for Double String Orchestra and Vaughan Williams’s The Lark Ascending, followed post-interval by Adès’s Märchentänze and Sibelius’s Fifth Symphony. A calculated mix of more and less familiar works, certainly – but an otherwise unlikely foursome. The common preoccupations with folk music (threaded jauntily through the Tippett and the Adès) and the natural world (VW’s lark, Sibelius’s swans) only take us so far. In practice, the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra’s performance under its chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth revealed a shared creative tussle with existing musical forms and with finding new means of expression without breaking entirely with the old ways.The Lark Ascending thus abandoned the Smooth Classics at Seven-mode for a covered, sometimes icy sound in the BSO’s world-class strings and a more risk-taking, more improvisatory approach from soloist Anthony Marwood. The tone of his Stradivarius was expensively sweet and his cool, no-vibrato opening compelling, though his performance was marred by intonation problems. Marwood fared better in Adès’s Märchentänze, which reworks folk tunes with unexpected timbral combinations and harmonies, and where the solo line tangles deliciously with the orchestra’s violins. But this work, written for the ultra-charismatic violinist Pekka Kuusisto, was rather less interesting without such a compelling soloist. Continue reading...

title: The Guardian view on England's north-south divide: Burnham must deliver more than devolution | Editorial
desc: The prime minister promises to repair decades of regional damage. By 2024, that gap had more than tripled to 42%. What happened in the four decades that left younger adults in northern England with so much worse chances of survival?The answer lies in the lives and jobs that people have, and the homes they can afford, as well as the state of the public services, like the NHS, that they rely on. Deindustrialisation stripped secure employment from many communities in the north of England – as it did in Scotland and Wales. Austerity then weakened support systems. title: What would make neonatal units safer for babies? | Letters
desc: Dr Pamela S Melding highlights how New Zealand has created a healthcare culture where patient safety, interests and consent are the overriding principles. Plus letters from Mark Hanson, Paul Whiteing and a reader who lost her babyI support Mark McDonald’s submission that the Thirlwall recommendations will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS (17 October). We often hear of hospital scandals where trusts are intent on preserving their reputations, internal inquiries go nowhere, defensive clinical staff deflect blame on to others, non‑disclosure to patients of errors and “lessons learned” rhetoric that is quickly forgotten. There is also an industry of ambulance-chasing lawyers. None of this is conducive to a no-blame, honest, open culture in healthcare. The Thirlwall recommendations of more surveillance will make it worse.There is an alternative. Most of my professional life as a hospital consultant, clinical director and deputy chief medical officer has been spent in New Zealand, whose publicly funded NHS is the same model as the UK’s – but with a major difference. In the 1970s, New Zealanders lost their right to sue for damages for medical accidents or injury through the public court system with the Accident Compensation Act. This got rid of the grievance culture and ambulance-chasers, and the system provided remedial care for any injury. In the 80s, after a huge scandal regarding medical investigations, the Cartwright inquiry ushered in the creation of the independent Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC) and overriding principles of patient safety, interests and consent.
